citation.title: Exact Bias Correction for Linear Adjustment of Randomized Controlled Trials

standing_assumptions:
Setting, notation and standing assumptions, as printed. Every passage was read from the rendered page images (staged/pages/p-NN.png, and 220 dpi renderings of the same PDF pages for subscripts and primes). Pages are those of Econometrica, Vol. 92, No. 5 (September, 2024), 1503–1519, with the PDF page in parentheses (PDF p. 1 is the journal's cover sheet, so printed page = PDF page + 1501). Appendix A (pp. 1510–1512) and Appendix B (pp. 1512–1519) are inside the article; there is no supplement.
[Setting: Section 2, p. 1504 (PDF p. 3)] “We follow the setting of Freedman (2008a), Lin (2013), Abadie, Athey, Imbens, and Wooldridge (2020), and Lei and Ding (2021), which assume a Neyman model with covariates (Splawa-Neyman, Dabrowska, and Speed (1923)). There are $n$ subjects indexed by $i = 1, \ldots, n$. For each subject, we observe an outcome $Y_i$ and a column vector of covariates $x_i = (x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \ldots, x_{id})' \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Each subject has two potential outcomes $y_i(1)$ and $y_i(0)$. We observe $Y_i = y_i(1)$ if subject $i$ is assigned to the treatment arm $T$, and $Y_i = y_i(0)$ if subject $i$ is assigned to the control arm $C$. Let $D_i$ be a binary variable, where $D_i = 1$ indicates that subject $i$ is assigned to the treatment arm.”
[Design: p. 1505 (PDF p. 4)] “The experiment is assumed to be completely randomized, where $n_T$ out of $n$ subjects are randomly assigned to the treatment arm $T$ and the remaining $n_C = n - n_T$ subjects are assigned to the control arm $C$. Random assignment is the sole source of randomness in our statistical analysis. The potential outcomes and covariates are considered fixed, and the bias of an estimator is assessed relative to the randomization distribution of the estimator. We do not assume the existence of a superpopulation: the $n$ subjects are the population of interest.”
[Notation: p. 1505 (PDF p. 4)] “We define $[T]$ as the set of subjects chosen for the treatment arm, given by $\{i \mid D_i = 1\}$, and similarly $[C]$ as the set of subjects chosen for the control arm, given by $\{i \mid D_i = 0\}$. For a possibly matrix-valued variable $a_i$, we use the notation $\bar a = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i$ to represent the population average, $\bar a_T = \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}a_i$ to denote the treatment group average, and $\bar a_C = \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}a_i$ to denote the control group average. The average treatment effect (ATE) can be expressed in this notation as $\mathrm{ATE} = \overline{y(1)} - \overline{y(0)}$, and the difference-in-means estimator is given by $\overline{Y}_T - \overline{Y}_C$. Similarly, we can write $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_ix_i' = \overline{xx'}$ for $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(1)x_i = \overline{y(1)x}$ for $y_i(1) \in \mathbb{R}$ and $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$.”
[Assumptions: p. 1505 (PDF p. 4)] “We make the following assumptions throughout the paper, which are standard in the literature.” ASSUMPTION 1: “For all $n$, there exists a finite constant $K$ such that $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(1)^2 \le K$, $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i(0)^2 \le K$, $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n x_{ik}^2 \le K$, for all $k = 1, \ldots, d$ and $d \le n$.” ASSUMPTION 2: “For all $n$ large enough, (1) $\bar x = 0$, and (2) $\overline{xx'} = I_d$, the $d \times d$ identity matrix.” ASSUMPTION 3: “Let $p_{T,n} = \frac{n_T}{n}$ and $p_{C,n} = \frac{n-n_T}{n}$ denote the inclusion probabilities into the treatment arm $T$ and control arm $C$, respectively. There exist positive constants $p_{\min}$ and $p_{\max}$ such that $0 < p_{\min} < p_{\max} < 1$ and $p_{\min} < p_{T,n} < p_{\max}$ for all $n$.” Then: “We shall hereafter omit the $n$ subscript in $p_{T,n}$ and $p_{C,n}$, and write $p_T$ and $p_C$ unless otherwise noted.”
[The two estimators: pp. 1505–1506 (PDF pp. 4–5)] “The first estimator results from a OLS regression: $Y_i \sim \alpha + \tau D_i + x_i'\beta$, (1) where one regresses observed outcome $Y_i$ on the treatment indicator $D_i$ and covariates $x_i$. We denote the OLS estimators for this case as $(\widehat\alpha, \widehat\tau, \widehat\beta)$. The estimator $\widehat\tau$ is hereafter referred to as the noninteracted ATE estimator. The second estimator results from an interacted OLS regression where researchers expand the covariates by including terms interacting the treatment indicator and covariates: $Y_i \sim \alpha_I + \tau_ID_i + x_i'\beta_{I,C} + D_ix_i'\beta_{I,T}$. (2) We denote the OLS estimators for the interacted case as $(\widehat\alpha_I, \widehat\tau_I, \widehat\beta_{I,C}, \widehat\beta_{I,T})$. The estimator $\widehat\tau_I$ is hereafter referred to as the interacted ATE estimator.”
[Section 3 objects: p. 1506 (PDF p. 5)] “As shown in Lin (2013), the noninteracted ATE estimator can be written as $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}} = \overline{y(1)}_T - \overline{y(0)}_C - (\bar x_T'\widehat\beta - \bar x_C'\widehat\beta)$, (3) where $\widehat\beta$ is the OLS coefficient estimators for the covariates.” “The coefficient estimators $\widehat\beta$ can be algebraically written as $\widehat\beta = \widehat L^{-1}\widehat N$, where $\widehat L = I_d - p_T\bar x_T\bar x_T' - p_C\bar x_C\bar x_C'$ and $\widehat N = p_T(\overline{y(1)x}_T - \overline{y(1)}_T\bar x_T) + p_C(\overline{y(0)x}_C - \overline{y(0)}_C\bar x_C)$ by an application of the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem.” “The OLS coefficient estimators can be thought of as estimating the (finite) population coefficients $\beta^* = L^{-1}N$, where $L = I_d$ and $N = p_T\overline{y(1)x} + p_C\overline{y(0)x}$.” Footnote 4: “Note we shall hereafter assume for simplicity that all design matrices, $\widehat L$, are invertible. In the case of noninvertible design matrices, our debiased procedure will still work after choosing an arbitrary generalized inverse matrix and computing the ATE estimators accordingly.” “Let $y_i^*(1)$ and $y_i^*(0)$ be the centered potential outcomes, that is, $y_i^*(1) = y_i(1) - \overline{y(1)}$ and $y_i^*(0) = y_i(0) - \overline{y(0)}$. Denote the (rescaled) leverage of the $i$th subject as $h_i = \|x_i\|_2^2$. As in Lei and Ding (2021), we define the maximum leverage as $\kappa = \max_{i=1,\ldots,n}\frac{h_i}{n} = \max_{i=1,\ldots,n}\frac{\|x_i\|_2^2}{n}$. (4)”
[Section 4 objects: p. 1509 (PDF p. 8)] “We write the regression coefficient estimators of the pretreatment covariates in the interacted case as $\widehat\beta_{I,T} = \widehat L_T^{-1}\widehat N_T$ and $\widehat\beta_{I,C} = \widehat L_C^{-1}\widehat N_C$, and their (finite) population counterparts as $\beta_{I,T} = I_d^{-1}N_T$ and $\beta_{I,C} = I_d^{-1}N_C$, with $\widehat L_T = \overline{xx'}_T - \bar x_T\bar x_T'$, $\widehat N_T = \overline{y(1)x}_T - \overline{y(1)}_T\bar x_T$, $\widehat L_C = \overline{xx'}_C - \bar x_C\bar x_C'$, $\widehat N_C = \overline{y(0)x}_C - \overline{y(0)}_C\bar x_C$, $N_T = \overline{y(1)x}$, and $N_C = \overline{y(0)x}$. As shown in Lin (2013), the OLS regression-adjusted ATE estimator can be written as $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I = \overline{y(1)}_T - \overline{y(0)}_C - (\bar x_T'\widehat\beta_{I,T} - \bar x_C'\widehat\beta_{I,C})$ for the interacted case, where $\widehat\beta_{I,T}$ and $\widehat\beta_{I,C}$ are the OLS coefficients on covariates $D_ix_i$ and $x_i$, repsectively.”
[Appendix A objects: p. 1510 (PDF p. 9)] “We define the following three constants: $N_{\mathrm{TTT}} = \frac{(n-n_T)(n-2n_T)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_T^2} = \frac{n_C(n_C-n_T)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_T^2}$, $N_{\mathrm{CCC}} = \frac{(n-n_C)(n-2n_C)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_C^2} = \frac{n_T(n_T-n_C)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_C^2}$, $N_{\mathrm{TTC}} = -\frac{(n-2n_T)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_T} = \frac{n_T-n_C}{(n-1)(n-2)n_T}$.” “Let $a = (a_1, \ldots, a_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $b = (b_1, \ldots, b_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be arbitrary $n$-vectors with fixed elements. We define the covariance estimator for the treated group as $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(a,b) = \overline{ab}_T - \bar a_T\bar b_T$, and similarly for the control group as $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_C(a,b) = \overline{ab}_C - \bar a_C\bar b_C$.”
[Readings fixed by the printed text and used in every target] (a) $\mathbf{E}$ (also printed $E$), $\mathrm{Var}$ and all probability statements refer to the randomization distribution: $[T]$ is uniformly distributed over the $\binom{n}{n_T}$ subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ of size $n_T$, $[C]$ is its complement, both arms are non-empty ($1 \le n_T \le n-1$), and everything else is fixed. (b) Vectors are column vectors and a prime is a transpose; for $n$-vectors $a$, $b$ of scalars, $\overline{ab}$ is the average of the products $a_ib_i$, so $\overline{hy(1)}_T - \bar h_T\overline{y(1)}_T = \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(h, y(1))$, and $\overline{hy(1)} - \bar h\times\overline{y(1)}$ is the finite-population covariance of $h$ and $y(1)$ with divisor $n$. (c) $I_d^{-1}$ is printed for $I_d$ throughout, and the paper prints both $\hat N$ and $\widehat N$ (also $\hat N_T$, $\widehat N_T$) for the same objects. (d) In Assumption 1, $K$ is one constant, the same for every $n$: this is the reading the proofs use (the printed order of quantifiers is the clarity note P005-N002, not an error). (e) Assumption 2 is printed “for all $n$ large enough”; an exact finite-sample statement is read at a fixed $n$ at which (1) and (2) hold. Under Assumption 2, $\bar h = \frac1n\sum_i\|x_i\|_2^2 = \mathrm{tr}(\overline{xx'}) = d$, $h_i \le n$, and $\frac dn \le \kappa \le 1$ (the paper uses “$\kappa \in [\frac dn, 1]$” on p. 1516). (f) In Section 4, $\widehat\beta_{I,T}$ and $\widehat\beta_{I,C}$ are the within-arm slope vectors $\widehat L_T^{-1}\widehat N_T$ and $\widehat L_C^{-1}\widehat N_C$ defined there; their description as the coefficients on $D_ix_i$ and $x_i$ does not match parameterization (2), under which the coefficient on $D_ix_i$ is the difference of the two arm slopes (clarity note P005-E004, not an error). Every target uses the Section 4 definitions. (g) “Design matrices … are invertible” (footnote 4) is read as: $\widehat L$ (Section 3), respectively $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ (Section 4), is invertible under every assignment. (h) $O_p$, $o_p$, $O$, $o$ refer to a sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$, in which $d = d_n$, $n_T = n_{T,n}$, the covariates and the potential outcomes may all change with $n$; $\log$ is the natural logarithm.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Lemma A.1, the variance bound, as printed for arbitrary $n$-vectors $a$, $b$. The witness is the validator's and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 1511 (PDF p. 10), Appendix A.2; the vectors $a$, $b$ and the covariance estimators are introduced on p. 1510 (PDF p. 9)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 1510 (PDF p. 9), Appendix A.2] “Let $a = (a_1, \ldots, a_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $b = (b_1, \ldots, b_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be arbitrary $n$-vectors with fixed elements. We define the covariance estimator for the treated group as $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(a,b) = \overline{ab}_T - \bar a_T\bar b_T$, and similarly for the control group as $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_C(a,b) = \overline{ab}_C - \bar a_C\bar b_C$. The following lemma characterizes the mean and variance of these covariance estimators.”
[Printed, p. 1511 (PDF p. 10)] “LEMMA A.1: Let $t \in \{T, C\}$ and $n \ge 4$. Then, $$\mathbf{E}\big[\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_t(a,b)\big] = \frac{(n_t-1)n}{n_t(n-1)}(\overline{ab} - \bar a\bar b),$$ $$\mathrm{Var}\big(\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_t(a,b)\big) \le \frac{2(n-n_t)}{n_t(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(a_ib_i-\overline{ab})^2 + \frac{2(n-n_t)n}{n_t^3(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 \times \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2.$$”
[Counterexample to the variance bound] Take $n = 6$, $t = T$, $n_T = 4$ (so $n_C = 2$), $a = (0, -3, -1, 2, -4, -3)$ and $b = (2, 1, 3, -3, 1, 1)$. Every hypothesis of the lemma holds: $a$ and $b$ are fixed vectors in $\mathbb{R}^6$, $t \in \{T, C\}$, $n = 6 \ge 4$, and the treated group is a uniformly chosen subset of size 4 (15 equally likely subsets). Then:
(i) $\bar a = -\frac32$, $\bar b = \frac56$, $\overline{ab} = -\frac{19}{6}$, $\overline{ab} - \bar a\bar b = -\frac{23}{12}$, and $\mathbf{E}[\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(a,b)] = -\frac{69}{40} = \frac{(n_T-1)n}{n_T(n-1)}(\overline{ab} - \bar a\bar b)$: the expectation identity of the lemma holds.
(ii) $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(a,b)) = \frac{16607}{4800}$.
(iii) The printed right-hand side equals $\frac15\cdot\frac{113}{36} + \frac{3}{40}\cdot\frac{13}{2}\cdot\frac{25}{6} = \frac{113}{180} + \frac{65}{32} = \frac{3829}{1440}$, where $\frac{2(n-n_T)}{n_T(n-1)} = \frac15$, $\frac{2(n-n_T)n}{n_T^3(n-1)} = \frac{3}{40}$, $\frac1n\sum_i(a_ib_i - \overline{ab})^2 = \frac{113}{36}$, $\frac1n\sum_ia_i^2 = \frac{13}{2}$ and $\frac1n\sum_ib_i^2 = \frac{25}{6}$.
(iv) $\frac{16607}{4800} - \frac{3829}{1440} = \frac{11531}{14400} > 0$, so $\mathrm{Var}(\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(a,b))$ exceeds the printed bound: the variance inequality of Lemma A.1 is false for this instance.
(v) [Why it fails] The left-hand side is unchanged when constants are added to $a$ and to $b$; the printed right-hand side is not. With $a^c = a - \bar a$ and $b^c = b - \bar b$, $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(a^c, b^c) = \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(a, b)$ for each of the 15 subsets, and the printed right-hand side evaluated at $(a^c, b^c)$ is $\frac{835}{128} \ge \frac{16607}{4800}$.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Lemma A.1, as repaired: the variance bound with centred vectors (Sol's smallest repair and the validator's derivation)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] Lemma A.1 and the definition of the covariance estimators, as transcribed in P005-T1. [Printed, proof of Lemma A.1, p. 1511] “To upper-bound the variance, we first note that the covariance estimator is location invariant and we can assume, without loss of generality, $\bar a = 0$ and $\bar b = 0$.$^{9}$ We then have $$\mathrm{Var}(\overline{ab}_T - \bar a_T\bar b_T) \le 2\,\mathrm{Var}(\overline{ab}_T) + 2\,\mathrm{Var}(\bar a_T\bar b_T) = 2\,\mathrm{Var}(\overline{ab}_T) + \frac{2}{n_T^4}\mathrm{Var}\Big(\sum_{i,j\in[T]}a_ib_j\Big)$$ $$\le \frac{2(n-n_T)}{n_T(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(a_ib_i-\overline{ab})^2 + \frac{2(n-n_T)n}{n_T^3(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\,\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2,$$ where the last inequality follows from the variance calculation of simple random samplings (first term) and Lemma A.5 in Lei and Ding (2021) (second term).” Footnote 9: “This is required by the conditions of Lemma A.5 in Lei and Ding (2021).”
[Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P005-E002, smallest_repair), verbatim, first part] “For arbitrary fixed $a,b$, define $a_i^c=a_i-\bar a$ and $b_i^c=b_i-\bar b$. Keep the printed expectation identity. For $m=n_t$ and $n\ge4$, the variance bound is \[\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}_t(a,b))\le\frac{2(n-m)}{m(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_i(a_i^c b_i^c-\overline{a^c b^c})^2+\frac{2(n-m)n}{m^3(n-1)}\left(\frac1n\sum_i(a_i^c)^2\right)\left(\frac1n\sum_i(b_i^c)^2\right).\]”
[Corrected statement, with every hypothesis] Let $n \ge 4$, $1 \le n_T \le n-1$ and $n_C = n - n_T$; let $[T]$ be uniformly distributed over the subsets of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ of size $n_T$ and $[C]$ its complement; let $t \in \{T, C\}$; let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be arbitrary fixed vectors and put $a_i^c = a_i - \bar a$, $b_i^c = b_i - \bar b$. Then
(i) $\mathbf{E}\big[\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_t(a,b)\big] = \frac{(n_t-1)n}{n_t(n-1)}(\overline{ab} - \bar a\bar b)$ (as printed; it needs no centring);
(ii) $\mathrm{Var}\big(\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_t(a,b)\big) \le \frac{2(n-n_t)}{n_t(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\big(a_i^cb_i^c - \overline{a^cb^c}\big)^2 + \frac{2(n-n_t)n}{n_t^3(n-1)}\Big(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(a_i^c)^2\Big)\Big(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(b_i^c)^2\Big)$.
Equivalently: the printed bound holds for all $a$, $b$ with $\bar a = 0$ and $\bar b = 0$, and for general $a$, $b$ after both vectors are centred on its right-hand side.
[The steps of the validator's proof; each is an exact statement for fixed $n \ge 4$ and $m = n_t$, with $S$ a uniform subset of size $m$, $u = a^c$, $v = b^c$]
(a) Location invariance: $\overline{ab}_S - \bar a_S\bar b_S = \overline{uv}_S - \bar u_S\bar v_S$ for every subset $S$.
(b) $\mathrm{Var}(\overline{uv}_S) = \frac{n-m}{m(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_i(u_iv_i - \overline{uv})^2$ (the variance of a sample mean under simple random sampling).
(c) Let $Z = (\sum_{i\in S}u_i)(\sum_{i\in S}v_i)$, $A = \sum_iu_i^2$, $B = \sum_iv_i^2$, $G = \sum_iu_iv_i$, $H = \sum_iu_i^2v_i^2$, $\alpha = \frac{m(n-m)}{n(n-1)}$ and $\ell = \frac{m(m-1)(n-m)(n-m-1)}{n(n-1)(n-2)(n-3)}$. Because $\sum_iu_i = \sum_iv_i = 0$: $\mathbf{E}Z = \alpha G$ and $\mathrm{Var}\,Z = (\alpha - 6\ell)H + \ell AB + (2\ell - \alpha^2)G^2 \le \alpha AB$. Hence $\mathrm{Var}(\bar u_S\bar v_S) = m^{-4}\,\mathrm{Var}\,Z \le \frac{(n-m)n}{m^3(n-1)}\big(\frac1n\sum_iu_i^2\big)\big(\frac1n\sum_iv_i^2\big)$. (This is the step the paper takes from Lemma A.5 of Lei and Ding (2021); it requires centred vectors, as footnote 9 says.)
(d) $\mathrm{Var}(U - V) \le 2\,\mathrm{Var}(U) + 2\,\mathrm{Var}(V)$, applied with $U = \overline{uv}_S$ and $V = \bar u_S\bar v_S$; with (a)–(c) this gives (ii).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As in P005-T1: [p. 1505 (PDF p. 4)] complete randomization and the bar notation; [p. 1510 (PDF p. 9)] $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(a,b) = \overline{ab}_T - \bar a_T\bar b_T$, $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_C(a,b) = \overline{ab}_C - \bar a_C\bar b_C$. $a^c$, $b^c$ (Sol's notation) are the vectors centred at their population means; $\overline{a^cb^c} = \frac1n\sum_ia_i^cb_i^c = \overline{ab} - \bar a\bar b$. $Z, A, B, G, H, \alpha, \ell$ are the validator's notation.
canonical_claim.note: From Sol's smallest_repair and prior_correction.corrected_text for P005-E002 (the earlier correction is judged correct) and section 3 of the validator's derivation, which proves (ii) for every $n \ge 4$ without the external citation; the three coefficient identities $p_1 - p_2 = \alpha$, $p_2 - 2p_3 + p_4 = \ell$, $p_1 - 7p_2 + 12p_3 - 6p_4 = \alpha - 6\ell$ (with $p_r$ the inclusion probability of $r$ distinct units) are also checked symbolically in check.py. Repair cost: none (no new assumption, no change of estimator or of rate). The lemma prints only “$n \ge 4$”; both arms non-empty is the paper's setting, and for $n_t = 1$ the estimator is identically zero. The second part of Sol's repair, the corrected application on p. 1517, is P005-T4.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Theorem 3.2 (Appendix B.2), item 2: the chain “First notice, by Lemma A.1 and Assumption 1, …”, as printed. The witness is the validator's and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed, p. 1517 (PDF p. 16), proof of Theorem 3.2, item 2] “2. Since the first-order term in (11) is canceled, we characterize the variance of the form $\frac1n(\overline{hy(1)}_T - \bar h_T\overline{y(1)}_T)$. First notice, by Lemma A.1 and Assumption 1, $$\mathrm{Var}\big[(\overline{hy(1)}_T - \bar h_T\overline{y(1)}_T)\big] \le \frac{2(n-n_T)}{n_T(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\big(h_iy_i(1)-\overline{hy(1)}\big)^2 + \frac{2(n-n_T)n}{n_T^3(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2(1)\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n h_i^2$$ $$\le \frac{2(n-n_T)}{n_T(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n h_i^2y_i^2(1) + \frac{2(n-n_T)n}{n_T^3(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2(1)\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n h_i^2$$ $$\le \frac{2(n-n_T)}{n_T(n-1)}n^2\kappa^2\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2(1) + \frac{2(n-n_T)n}{n_T^3(n-1)}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2(1)\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n h_i\times n\kappa = O\Big(\kappa^2n+\frac{\kappa d}{n}\Big).$$ Thus, $\mathrm{Var}\big(\frac1n(\overline{hy(1)}_T - \bar h_T\overline{y(1)}_T)\big) = O\big(\frac{\kappa^2}{n}+\frac{\kappa d}{n^3}\big)$.”
[Counterexample to the first inequality of the chain, with an admissible leverage vector] Take $n = 16$, $n_T = n_C = 8$, $d = 1$, $c = \sqrt{8/71}$, $x = (8c, -8c, c, -c, c, -c, \ldots, c, -c)$ (two units with $|x_i| = 8c$ followed by seven pairs $(c, -c)$), $y(1) = (\frac{1}{64}, \frac{1}{64}, 1, \ldots, 1)$ and $y(0) = (0, \ldots, 0)$. Then:

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] Theorem 4.1 begins “THEOREM 4.1: Under Assumptions 1–3, …” on p. 1509 (PDF p. 8). [Printed, continuation of Theorem 4.1 on p. 1510 (PDF p. 9)] “If $\kappa\log d = o(1)$,$^{8}$ $$\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I = \mathrm{ATE} + \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}\big(y_i(1) - \overline{y(1)} - x_i'\beta_{I,T}\big) - \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}\big(y_i(0) - \overline{y(0)} - x_i'\beta_{I,C}\big) + O_p\Big(\sqrt{\frac{\kappa d}{n}}\Big).$$” Footnote 8: “The upper bound on the stochastic order of the bias of the interacted case is characterized in equation (15) in Lei and Ding (2021).”
[Counterexample: a sequence with one covariate] For every integer $n \ge 6$ let $d = 1$, $n_T = \lfloor n/2\rfloor$, $n_C = n - n_T$, $\epsilon = n^{-2}$, and $v_1 = 0$, $v_{j+2} = -1 + \frac{2j}{n-2}$ for $j = 0, \ldots, n-2$. Put $a_1 = 1$ and $a_i = \epsilon v_i$ for $i \ge 2$; $y_i(1) = y_i(0) = v_i$; $z_i = a_i - \frac1n$; $q = \frac1n\sum_iz_i^2$; and $x_i = z_i/\sqrt q$. Then:
(i) [The hypotheses of the theorem hold] $\sum_iv_i = 0$, $\sum_iv_i^2 = \frac{n(n-1)}{3(n-2)}$, $\bar a = \frac1n$ and $q = \frac{n-1}{n^2}\big(1 + \frac{1}{3(n-2)n^2}\big) > 0$. Hence $\bar x = 0$ and $\overline{x^2} = 1$ for every $n \ge 6$ (Assumption 2); $|y_i(1)| = |y_i(0)| \le 1$ and $\frac1n\sum_ix_i^2 = 1$ (Assumption 1 with $K = 1$ for all $n$); $\frac14 < n_T/n < \frac34$ (Assumption 3). Under every assignment each arm has at least three units and positive within-arm variance of $x$, so $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$ are invertible (footnote 4). $\mathrm{ATE} = 0$.
(ii) [Leverage] $\kappa = \frac{(1 - 1/n)^2}{nq} = \frac{3n(n-1)(n-2)}{3n^2(n-2)+1} \to 1$, while $\kappa\log d = \kappa\log1 = 0$ for every $n$. So the printed condition $\kappa\log d = o(1)$ holds although $\kappa$ does not tend to 0.
(iii) [The estimator; even $n \ge 6$, so $n_T = n_C = n/2$] $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I = (\overline{y(1)}_T - \bar x_T'\widehat\beta_{I,T}) - (\overline{y(0)}_C - \bar x_C'\widehat\beta_{I,C})$ is the difference of the two within-arm fitted lines evaluated at $x = 0$, that is, at $a = \frac1n$. In the arm that does not contain unit 1, $y_i = a_i/\epsilon$ exactly, so its fitted value at $a = \frac1n$ is $\frac{1}{n\epsilon} = n$. In the arm that contains unit 1 the fitted slope $s_H$ in the coordinate $a$ satisfies $|s_H| \le 2$ and the fitted value $p_H$ at $a = \frac1n$ satisfies $|p_H| \le \frac{25}{18}$. Hence $|\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I| \ge n - 3$ under every assignment.
(iv) [The leading term] $\beta_{I,T} = \beta_{I,C} = \sqrt q\,b$ with $b = \frac{\sum_iz_iv_i}{\sum_iz_i^2} = \frac{n^2}{3n^2(n-2)+1} \le \frac{1}{12}$, so that $y_i(t) - \overline{y(t)} - x_i'\beta_{I,t} = v_i - bz_i =: e_i$ for $t = 0, 1$, with $|e_i| \le \frac{13}{12}$. The printed leading term is $L_n = \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}e_i - \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}e_i$, and $|L_n| \le \frac{13}{6} < 3$ under every assignment.
(v) [The remainder] $R_n := \widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I - \mathrm{ATE} - L_n$ satisfies $|R_n| \ge n - 6$ under every assignment, for every even $n \ge 6$, whereas $\sqrt{\kappa d/n} \le n^{-1/2}$. Hence $|R_n|\big/\sqrt{\kappa d/n} \ge (n-6)\sqrt n \to \infty$ with probability one along the even integers: for every $M$, $\Pr\big(|R_n| > M\sqrt{\kappa d/n}\big) = 1$ for all large even $n$. So $R_n$ is not $O_p\big(\sqrt{\kappa d/n}\big)$, and the printed expansion fails for this sequence.
(vi) [Exact values for checking] $n = 6$: $\kappa = \frac{360}{433}$, $b = \frac{36}{433}$, and the minimum of $|R_n|$ over the 20 assignments is $\frac{4357386}{779833} \approx 5.59$. $n = 12$: $\kappa = \frac{3960}{4321}$, $b = \frac{144}{4321}$, and the minimum of $|R_n|$ over the 924 assignments is $\frac{8690712840}{752921287} \approx 11.54$.

[Design and notation, p. 1505 (PDF p. 4)] “The experiment is assumed to be completely randomized, where $n_T$ out of $n$ subjects are randomly assigned to the treatment arm $T$ and the remaining $n_C = n - n_T$ subjects are assigned to the control arm $C$.” $[T] = \{i \mid D_i = 1\}$, $[C] = \{i \mid D_i = 0\}$; $\bar a = \frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n a_i$, $\bar a_T = \frac{1}{n_T}\sum_{i\in[T]}a_i$, $\bar a_C = \frac{1}{n_C}\sum_{i\in[C]}a_i$ for a possibly matrix-valued $a_i$; $\mathrm{ATE} = \overline{y(1)} - \overline{y(0)}$; $\overline{xx'} = \frac1n\sum_i x_ix_i'$, $\overline{y(1)x} = \frac1n\sum_i y_i(1)x_i$. $\mathbf{E}$, $\mathrm{Var}$ and probabilities are over the assignment, uniform on the $\binom{n}{n_T}$ subsets $[T]$ of size $n_T$; potential outcomes and covariates are fixed.

There exist positive constants $p_{\min}$ and $p_{\max}$ such that $0 < p_{\min} < p_{\max} < 1$ and $p_{\min} < p_{T,n} < p_{\max}$ for all $n$.” ($p_T$, $p_C$ are written without the subscript $n$.)
[Section 4, p. 1509 (PDF p. 8)] “We write the regression coefficient estimators of the pretreatment covariates in the interacted case as $\widehat\beta_{I,T} = \widehat L_T^{-1}\widehat N_T$ and $\widehat\beta_{I,C} = \widehat L_C^{-1}\widehat N_C$, and their (finite) population counterparts as $\beta_{I,T} = I_d^{-1}N_T$ and $\beta_{I,C} = I_d^{-1}N_C$, with $\widehat L_T = \overline{xx'}_T - \bar x_T\bar x_T'$, $\widehat N_T = \overline{y(1)x}_T - \overline{y(1)}_T\bar x_T$, $\widehat L_C = \overline{xx'}_C - \bar x_C\bar x_C'$, $\widehat N_C = \overline{y(0)x}_C - \overline{y(0)}_C\bar x_C$, $N_T = \overline{y(1)x}$, and $N_C = \overline{y(0)x}$. As shown in Lin (2013), the OLS regression-adjusted ATE estimator can be written as $\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I = \overline{y(1)}_T - \overline{y(0)}_C - (\bar x_T'\widehat\beta_{I,T} - \bar x_C'\widehat\beta_{I,C})$ for the interacted case”. $y^*$, $h$, $\kappa$ and footnote 4 (invertibility of the design matrices, here $\widehat L_T$ and $\widehat L_C$) as in Section 3, p. 1506 (PDF p. 5): $y_i^*(t) = y_i(t) - \overline{y(t)}$, $h_i = \|x_i\|_2^2$, $\kappa = \max_i h_i/n$.
For $d = 1$: $\widehat L_T = \overline{x^2}_T - \bar x_T^2$, $\widehat N_T = \overline{y(1)x}_T - \overline{y(1)}_T\bar x_T$, $\widehat\beta_{I,T} = \widehat N_T/\widehat L_T$ (the within-arm least-squares slope), and likewise for $C$; $\beta_{I,T} = \overline{y(1)x}$, $\beta_{I,C} = \overline{y(0)x}$. The validator's symbols $v, a, z, q, b, e, s_H, p_H, L_n, R_n$ are defined in the statement; the regression on $x$ is an affine reparameterization of the regression on $a$, so all quantities in (iii)–(vi) are rational although $x_i = z_i/\sqrt q$ is not. [Reading of the order symbols] A sequence of finite populations indexed by $n$: for each $n$, a dimension $d = d_n$ with $1 \le d_n \le n$, covariates $x_1,\ldots,x_n \in \mathbb{R}^{d_n}$, potential outcomes $y_i(1), y_i(0)$ and an arm size $n_T = n_{T,n}$, all of which may change with $n$; Assumption 1 holds with one constant $K$ for all $n$, Assumption 2 for all $n$ large enough, Assumption 3 with fixed $p_{\min}, p_{\max}$; the design matrices are invertible under every assignment (footnote 4). For random variables $R_n$ on the randomization spaces and positive numbers $r_n$: $R_n = O_p(r_n)$ means that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are $M < \infty$ and $n_0$ with $\Pr(|R_n| > Mr_n) < \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge n_0$; $R_n = o_p(r_n)$ means that $\Pr(|R_n| > \delta r_n) \to 0$ for every $\delta > 0$.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: Exact statements for each fixed $n$, from sections 2–5 of the validator's derivation: (1) $\sum_iv_i = 0$ and $\sum_iv_i^2 = \frac{n(n-1)}{3(n-2)}$; $q = \frac{n-1}{n^2}\big(1 + \frac{1}{3(n-2)n^2}\big)$; $\kappa = \frac{3n(n-1)(n-2)}{3n^2(n-2)+1}$. (2) The pairwise form of a least-squares slope: for an arm $H$, $s_H = \frac{\sum_{i<j;\,i,j\in H}(a_i - a_j)(v_i - v_j)}{\sum_{i<j;\,i,j\in H}(a_i - a_j)^2}$. (3) For even $n \ge 6$, $m = n/2$ and the arm $H$ containing unit 1: $|s_H| \le \frac{(m-1)(1+\epsilon) + 2\epsilon(m-1)(m-2)}{(m-1)(1-\epsilon)^2} = \frac{1 + (n-3)/n^2}{(1 - 1/n^2)^2} \le \frac{1404}{1225} < 2$; $|\bar v_H| \le 1$; $|\bar a_H - \frac1n| \le \frac1n + \epsilon \le \frac{7}{36}$; hence $|p_H| = |\bar v_H + s_H(\frac1n - \bar a_H)| \le \frac{25}{18}$. (4) In the arm without unit 1, $v_i = a_i/\epsilon$ for every unit, so the fitted line is $a \mapsto a/\epsilon$ and its value at $a = \frac1n$ is $n$. (5) $b = \frac{\epsilon\sum_iv_i^2}{nq} = \frac{n^2}{3n^2(n-2)+1} \le \frac{1}{3(n-2)} \le \frac{1}{12}$; $|z_i| < 1$, $|v_i| \le 1$, so $|e_i| \le \frac{13}{12}$ and $|L_n| \le \frac{13}{6}$. (6) $|R_n| \ge |\widehat{\mathrm{ATE}}_I| - |L_n| \ge (n - \frac{25}{18}) - \frac{13}{6} \ge n - 6$. The asymptotic conclusion is then the elementary fact that a sequence with $|R_n|/r_n \ge (n-6)\sqrt n$ surely along a subsequence is not $O_p(r_n)$.
canonical_claim.note: From sections 2–5 of the first validator's derivation (the sequence is Sol's E4), with exact rational enumeration of all assignments at $n = 6, 8, 10, 12, 14$ (check.py, exact_output.json); (i), (ii), (iv), (vi) and the bounds of (iii), (v) were re-run in exact arithmetic for $n = 6, 8, 10, 12$ when this target was fixed. (4) Exact form of the remainder: $R_n = -\bar x_T'\widehat L_T^{-1}\big(\overline{xe(1)}_T - \bar x_T\overline{e(1)}_T\big) + \bar x_C'\widehat L_C^{-1}\big(\overline{xe(0)}_C - \bar x_C\overline{e(0)}_C\big)$, where $e_i(t) = y_i(t) - \overline{y(t)} - x_i'\beta_{I,t}$. [Printed, same page, two displays earlier] “Collecting the constants in front of $(\overline{hy(1)}_T-\bar h_T\overline{y(1)}_T)$ gives $$\frac{n_C}{n(n_T-1)} - \frac{(n-n_T)(n-2n_T)}{(n-1)(n-2)n_T^2}\times\frac{n_T(n-1)}{(n_T-1)n} = \frac{n_C}{(n-2)n_T}.$$ Thus, an unbiased estimator for $\mathbf{E}[-\bar x_T'(\nu_{1T}+\nu_{2T}+\nu_{3T})]$ is $$-\frac{n_C}{(n-2)n_T}\big(\overline{hy(1)}_T-\bar h_T\overline{y(1)}_T\big) - \bar x_T'\big(\widehat L_T^{-1}-I_d^{-1}\big)\hat N_T.$$”

After the inverse cancels, the printed first and second lines equal $P := \overline{y(1)}_T - \bar x_T'\hat N_T + \frac{n_T}{(n-2)n_C}\big(\overline{hy(1)}_T - \bar h_T\overline{y(1)}_T\big)$ (reading the unprimed $\bar x_T$ as $\bar x_T'$: the missing transposes of P005-E010, restored in P005-T11), whereas the estimator derived two displays earlier gives $Q := \overline{y(1)}_T - \bar x_T'\hat N_T + \frac{n_C}{(n-2)n_T}\big(\overline{hy(1)}_T - \bar h_T\overline{y(1)}_T\big)$.

(ii) With the printed weight $\frac{n_T}{(n-2)n_C} = \frac18$: $\mathbf{E}[P] = \frac{4913}{1200} \ne \frac{20}{3} = \overline{y(1)}$.
(iii) With the derived weight $\frac{n_C}{(n-2)n_T} = \frac12$: $\mathbf{E}[Q] = \frac{20}{3} = \overline{y(1)}$.
(iv) $P - Q = \big(\frac{n_T}{(n-2)n_C} - \frac{n_C}{(n-2)n_T}\big)\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(h, y(1)) = -\frac38\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(h, y(1))$, and $\mathbf{E}[P] - \mathbf{E}[Q] = -\frac38\cdot\frac{(n_T-1)n}{n_T(n-1)}S_1 = -\frac38\cdot\frac35\cdot\frac{343}{30} = -\frac{1029}{400}$.
(In rational terms: $\bar x_T'\hat N_T = \frac{3}{20}\,\bar a_T\big(\overline{ay(1)}_T - \bar a_T\overline{y(1)}_T\big)$ and $\widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_T(h, y(1)) = \frac{3}{20}\big(\overline{a^2y(1)}_T - \overline{a^2}_T\overline{y(1)}_T\big)$.)
